text: A person types a single sentence describing the song they imagine, and a minute later a complete piece arrives, with a singer, instruments and a chorus that was never written by anyone. No musician was in the room, so what is the machine actually doing, and how can it produce something that sounds composed?

The first idea is to treat sound as language. A raw recording is far too detailed to predict directly, so an audio codec compresses it into a long sequence of small discrete units called tokens, much as a sentence is made of words. Once music is a sequence of tokens, it becomes something a language model knows how to handle.

The model is trained on a vast collection of recordings, each paired with a description, and its task is always the same: given the tokens so far, predict the next one. By doing this billions of times it absorbs how rhythm holds together, how a chord tends to follow another, and how a voice shapes a word, without being handed any rules of music theory.

Your prompt is the steering. The description of style is converted into numbers that guide every prediction, while lyrics, which can be written by a separate language model, tell the singer which syllables to place and when. The song is then generated one token after another, each choice shaped by everything that came before it and by what you asked for.

Tokens are only a code, so a decoder converts them back into an audible waveform, rebuilding the detail that the compression had set aside. This is why the result can feel so polished, and also why the same prompt gives a different song each time, because every prediction is a weighted draw among many plausible continuations.
A sentence, a model that has learned how music tends to unfold, and a decoder that turns that learning back into sound.
